mediaItem.keyStats: Troy Burner served 24 years, 8 months, and 22 days for a crime he did not commit.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of "Wrongful Conviction with Maggie Freeling" details the wrongful conviction of Troy Burner for the 1990 murder of Michael Wilson.  Despite having an alibi and no direct evidence linking him to the crime, Troy was implicated by informants seeking leniency in their own cases.  The prosecution relied on contradictory testimonies from these informants, leading to Troy's conviction and a 30-years-to-life sentence.  After nearly 25 years of incarceration, new evidence emerged, including a recantation from a key informant and alibi witnesses.  The Mid-Atlantic Innocence Project took on his case, and Troy was eventually released on time served in 2018 and fully exonerated in 2020.  His story highlights the dangers of unreliable informant testimony and the long fight for justice after wrongful conviction.  Since his release, Troy has become an advocate for criminal justice reform and found personal fulfillment.

contributingFactorsRaw: False testimony from informants (Antoine Payton, Antonio Johnson)
innocenceLawyersRaw: Frances Walters (former legal director of MAIP, now Attorney Advisor at Department of Justice Office of the Pardon Attorney)
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: On April 21, 1990, Michael Wilson and Joseph Kennard were ambushed by two masked gunmen. Michael Wilson was shot multiple times and died days later. He initially named "Lewis and Little Rick" as his attackers. The case went cold for three years.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Testimony of Antoine Payton, who initially said Troy was not present, then changed his story to place Troy at the scene without a gun, and finally testified he saw Troy with a gun.
Testimony of Antonio Johnson, who claimed Brakmoret bragged about ordering the shooting and that Troy's gun jammed.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes:
- Requested a separate trial from co-defendants, which was denied.
- Further details on trial defense strategy are not provided in the transcript.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Recantation affidavit from Antoine Payton admitting he lied about Troy's involvement and presence at the scene.
Affidavit from Rick (Ricarad) Harrod stating only he and Lou McCoy shot Michael Wilson and Troy was not involved.
Alibi witnesses who testified they were playing dice with Troy at the time of the shooting.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails:
- Lou McCoy (named by Michael Wilson and Rick Harrod)
- Rick Harrod (named by Michael Wilson and admitted his involvement in affidavit)

keyQuotesRaw: Troy Burner: "You know, I didn't have nothing to do with it, so, you know, and they're not going to be able to find nobody to say I had nothing to do with it. So, you know, I held on to that, you know, that belief where they say the truth says you're free."
Inmate in prison: "He said, I think there's you. He said, because since I've been here, I've been here in your name." (referring to Payton's recantation affidavit)
Cherie to Troy in hospital: "How are you going to come back in my life and just want to die on me? You can't be my husband if you die, right?"
systemicIssuesRaw: Over-reliance on incentivized informant testimony in criminal cases.
The phenomenon of contradictory and changing testimonies from informants.
Difficulties in challenging and overturning wrongful convictions, even with recantations and alibi evidence.
The lengthy time individuals can spend incarcerated before exoneration.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Reforming the use of informant testimony to require greater scrutiny and corroboration.
Improving processes for reviewing and acting upon recantations and new evidence in wrongful conviction cases.
Reducing the time it takes to achieve exoneration once credible evidence of innocence emerges.
personalNarrativeRaw: Troy Burner lost nearly 25 years of his life due to wrongful conviction, impacting his career aspirations and personal freedom.
Despite the injustice, Troy displayed resilience by studying law in prison and actively working on his case.
Upon exoneration, he dedicated himself to advocating for criminal justice reform and assisting others who have been wrongfully convicted.
He found love and built a family after his release, highlighting the possibility of rebuilding life after wrongful imprisonment.
